subject: anaesthesia
title: Inhalational Pharmacology: Minimum Alveolar Concentration and Partition Coefficients

steps.title: Definition of Standard MAC
steps.tx: **Minimum alveolar concentration definition** represents the steady-state end-tidal alveolar concentration of an inhalational anaesthetic vapor at one atmosphere (760 mmHg) that prevents purposeful skeletal movement in 50 percent of human subjects in response to a standard noxious surgical stimulus, such as a skin incision. MAC provides an indispensable standardized metric of inhalational anaesthetic potency, allowing direct comparative dosing between volatile agents.

steps.title: Comparative MAC Potency Values
steps.tx: **Comparative standard MAC values** at standard atmospheric pressure highlight stark differences in volatility and potency: nitrous oxide has a MAC of 104 to 105 percent (requiring a hyperbaric chamber to achieve full surgical anaesthesia as a solitary agent), desflurane has a MAC of 6.0 percent, sevoflurane has a MAC of 2.0 percent, isoflurane has a MAC of 1.15 to 1.2 percent, and halothane has a MAC of 0.75 percent.

steps.title: MAC Fractions and Endpoints
steps.tx: **Physiological MAC fraction endpoints** define distinct neurofunctional thresholds across the central nervous system: MAC-awake (0.3 to 0.5 MAC) is the alveolar concentration at which 50 percent of patients open their eyes to verbal command during recovery; MAC-intubation (1.3 to 1.5 MAC without muscle relaxants) permits tracheal intubation; and MAC-BAR (1.5 to 2.0 MAC) blocks adrenergic and cardiovascular autonomic reflex responses to surgical incision.

right.title: MAC-BAR (1.5 to 2.0 MAC)

steps.title: Factors Altering MAC Requirements
steps.tx: **Factors altering MAC requirements** systematically shift the dose-response curve: MAC increases with youth (peaks at six months of age), hyperthermia, hypernatraemia, acute central nervous system stimulant intoxication (amphetamines, cocaine), and chronic ethanol abuse. Conversely, MAC decreases with advancing age (falls approximately 6 percent per decade past age 40), hypothermia, hyponatraemia, pregnancy (due to progesterone), acute alcohol intoxication, co-administered opioids, and hypotension.

steps.title: Blood-Gas Partition Coefficient
steps.tx: **Blood-gas partition coefficient kinetics** govern the speed of anaesthetic induction and recovery. A low blood-gas partition coefficient means the agent is poorly soluble in blood, requiring very few molecules to dissolve in pulmonary capillary blood before partial pressure rises, driving rapid alveolar-to-arterial equilibrium and swift induction: desflurane (0.42) and nitrous oxide (0.47) act fastest, followed by sevoflurane (0.65), isoflurane (1.4), and halothane (2.4).

steps.title: Meyer-Overton Lipid Hypothesis
steps.tx: **Meyer-Overton unitary lipid hypothesis** demonstrates that the anaesthetic potency of an inhalational agent is directly proportional to its lipid solubility, represented by its oil-gas partition coefficient. Agents with high oil-gas partition coefficients dissolve readily in neuronal lipid bilayer membranes and hydrophobic protein pockets, requiring low alveolar concentrations to achieve anaesthesia: halothane (oil-gas 224, MAC 0.75%) is far more potent than desflurane (oil-gas 19, MAC 6.0%).

right.title: Low Oil-Gas Coefficient (Desflurane 19)

steps.title: Second Gas Effect Mechanism
steps.tx: **Second gas effect phenomenon** occurs when a high concentration of an insoluble first gas, specifically nitrous oxide (administered at 70 percent), is inhaled alongside a lower concentration of a volatile second gas, such as sevoflurane. Enormous rapid uptake of nitrous oxide from the alveolus into pulmonary capillary blood shrinks residual alveolar gas volume, concentrating the remaining second gas and accelerating its alveolar rise and arterial saturation.

steps.title: Cardiovascular and Respiratory Effects
steps.tx: **Systemic physiological profile of volatile agents** exhibits shared and agent-specific properties: all modern halogenated volatiles produce dose-dependent myocardial depression, blunted ventilatory response to hypercapnia and hypoxaemia, and cerebral vasodilation that raises cerebral blood flow. Isoflurane and desflurane cause peripheral vasodilation with preservation of cardiac output, while desflurane above 1 MAC produces transient sympathetic tachycardia from airway irritation.
